questions.question: Explain how the periodic table is organised, and show how the position of an element with configuration 1s two, 2s two, 2p six, 3s one is read from its electron structure.
questions.expected_answer: The table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number — proton count. A horizontal row is a period, and the period number equals the number of occupied energy levels. A vertical column is a group, and elements in a group share the same number of valence electrons, which is why they behave similarly; for groups 13 to 18 the units digit of the group number gives the valence count. The configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ uses three energy levels, so the element is in period 3, and it has one valence electron, so it is in group 1 — the element is sodium, an alkali metal that forms a plus-one ion.

questions.question: State the trends in atomic radius and ionisation energy across a period and down a group, giving the reason for each direction.
questions.expected_answer: Across a period, atomic radius decreases: protons are added to the nucleus while the outer electrons stay in the same level, so the stronger nuclear pull draws the electron cloud inward. Down a group, radius increases: each row adds a whole new occupied energy level, placing the outer electrons further from the nucleus. Ionisation energy — the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom — increases across a period, because the greater nuclear pull grips the outer electrons more tightly; it decreases down a group, because the outer electron is further away and screened by more inner levels, so it is removed more easily. Electron affinity and electronegativity follow the same logic, rising across a period and falling down a group; noble gases are excluded from the electronegativity trend because they rarely bond.

questions.question: Compare the reactivity trends of group 1 and group 17 as you move down each group, and explain why group 18 elements are unreactive.
questions.expected_answer: Group 1, the alkali metals, react by losing their single valence electron to form plus-one ions. Down the group the outer electron lies further from the nucleus and is screened by more inner levels, so it is lost more easily — reactivity increases down the group; potassium reacts more violently with water than sodium. Group 17, the halogens, react by gaining one electron to form minus-one ions. Down the group the weakened nuclear grip pulls incoming electrons less strongly, so reactivity decreases: fluorine is the most reactive halogen and iodine the least. The two trends mirror each other because the same weakening grip makes giving easier but taking harder. Group 18, the noble gases, have completely full outer energy levels — nothing to lose and nothing to gain — so they are chemically unreactive and exist as single atoms.
